name: Moral foundations theory
statement: Liberals rest moral judgement mainly on harm and fairness, while conservatives spread it more evenly across those two plus loyalty, authority and purity.
meaning: Graham, Haidt and Nosek call this the moral foundations hypothesis. It names five sets of moral intuitions: Harm/care, Fairness/reciprocity, Ingroup/loyalty, Authority/respect and Purity/sanctity. The first two are grouped as individualizing, the last three as binding. The prediction is not that conservatives are more moral or liberals less so. It is that the gap between the two groups of foundations is wider on the left than on the right. Two claims live under the one name and they carry separate evidence. The first is the political difference, measured as a correlation between where someone places themselves on a liberal to conservative scale and how morally relevant they rate each set of concerns. The second is the measurement model, the assertion that five distinct factors sit behind the items. A reader can accept the first and reject the second, and several research groups do.

origin.who: Jesse Graham, Jonathan Haidt and Brian A. Nosek
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Volume 96, issue 5, pages 1029 to 1046. The article presents four studies and credits the underlying theory to Haidt and Joseph (2004) and Haidt and Graham (2007), which it describes as work on moral differences across cultures rather than across a political spectrum. The 30-item Moral Foundations Questionnaire that later critics test came two years afterwards, in Graham, Nosek, Haidt, Iyer, Koleva and Ditto (2011). Study 1 here used 15 moral relevance items, and the 2009 paper says explicitly that developing or validating a scale was not its intention.

evidence: Study 1 gave 15 moral relevance items on a 6-point scale to 1,613 adults registered at Project Implicit, of whom 902 called themselves liberal, 366 moderate and 264 conservative. Sixty-five, 4.0%, were dropped for rating belief in astrology as morally relevant. Cronbach's alphas were .62 for Harm, .67 Fairness, .59 Ingroup, .39 Authority and .70 Purity. With age, gender, education and income in the model, political identity predicted all five foundations in the predicted direction, average absolute beta .25, range .16 to .34. Aggregated individualizing ratings exceeded binding ratings, F(1, 1207) = 1,895.09, partial eta-squared .61, and politics moderated that gap, F(1, 1207) = 224.34, partial eta-squared .16. Study 2 added moral judgement items for 2,212 United States volunteers. Political identity predicted judgements for Harm at beta -.32, Fairness -.43, Ingroup .67, Authority .62 and Purity .57, all p < .001. Study 3 asked 8,193 visitors to yourmorals.org what they would take to violate each foundation, with analyses on the 6,619 who placed themselves on the 7-point scale. Politics predicted Ingroup at beta .42, Authority .31 and Purity .11, and predicted Harm at .06 and Fairness at .07 in the direction opposite to prediction, all p < .001. Study 4 ran a 295-word dictionary over 69 Unitarian and 34 Southern Baptist sermons. Raw word counts contradicted the prediction for Ingroup, which liberal preachers used more. Four raters, reliability .79, scored 3,281 uses of the 23 most discriminating words in context, and that scoring reversed the Ingroup result.

replication.headline: Many Labs 2 repeated the questionnaire finding worldwide at about half the original size. A high-powered repeat of the sermon text analysis did not hold.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 was a multi-laboratory project, not one team. It ran 125 samples, 64 on slate 1 and 61 on slate 2 with 15 sites doing both, 15,305 participants, 39 samples from the United States and 86 from 35 other countries and territories. Graham, Haidt and Nosek's Study 1 sat on slate 1. The primary target was the tie between ideology and the binding foundations. In the aggregate sample of 6,966 the political right rated binding concerns as more morally relevant, r = 0.14, p = 6.05e-34, d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.25, 0.34], Cohen's q = 0.15, 95% CI [0.12, 0.17], against an original d of 0.52, 95% CI [0.40, 0.63]. The secondary test on individualizing concerns gave d = -0.27, 95% CI [-0.32, -0.22] on 6,970 participants, against an original -0.43. Median effect across samples was d = 0.23. In 25.00% of samples the effect reached significance in the expected direction, 75.00% were null and none ran the other way. Heterogeneity was real, Q(59) = 175.26, p < .001, I-squared 64%, 95% CI [49%, 75%], tau 0.09, and neither WEIRD against less WEIRD (Q = 0.25, p = 0.62) nor lab against online (Q = 1.26, p = 0.26) accounted for it. Kivikangas and colleagues meta-analysed 89 samples, 605 effect sizes and 33,804 independent participants alongside 192,870 from yourmorals.org. Correlations with self-placed conservatism were care r = -.146, 95% CI [-.168, -.123], fairness -.215 [-.239, -.191], loyalty .288 [.261, .315], authority .367 [.345, .390] and sanctity .372 [.347, .397]. They report the direction and the ordering as supported and heterogeneity as moderate, I-squared from 85.46% to 91.85%. The 95% prediction interval for care runs from -.320 to .029 and crosses zero. Estimates from yourmorals.org exceeded those from representative samples by as much as .253, which they read as inflation from self-selection. Frimer repeated the sermon analysis. His abstract reports two high-powered replications and six extensions, an average replication success rate of 30%, effect sizes 38 times smaller than the original, and a meta-analysis on 303,680 texts giving authority r = 0.05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.09], purity r = 0.14 [0.09, 0.19], loyalty r = -0.08 [-0.10, -0.05], harm r = 0.00 [-0.02, 0.02] and fairness r = -0.03 [-0.06, 0.01]. Loyalty ran opposite to the theory and harm and fairness sat at zero.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., Adams, B. G., Adams, R. B., Jr., Alper, S., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: The measurement model is where the argument is hottest, and it is a separate argument from the political one. Iurino and Saucier tested the 20-item short questionnaire across 27 countries and report that it is difficult to specify the items in a five-factor model that converges without problems across a wide range of populations. Harper and Rhodes ran the full 32-item questionnaire plus Iyer and colleagues' liberty items on British voters. A parallel analysis on 428 respondents pointed to five factors, but exploratory analysis yielded three usable clusters, which they named traditionalism, compassion and liberty. In an independent sample of 322 their three-factor model fitted at CFI .87, TLI .85, RMSEA .07, against CFI .73, TLI .70, RMSEA .08 for the five-factor questionnaire and CFI .66, TLI .64, RMSEA .08 for the six-factor version. They call the work exploratory, note that both samples were British, and cite Brandt, He and Bender for the position that failures of measurement invariance do not upset conclusions about ideological differences. The five-factor model has defenders. Davies, Sibley and Liu tested it in a New Zealand national probability sample of 3,994 against single-factor, two-factor, three-factor and hierarchical rivals, and report that it provided a reasonable fit. Wormley, Scott, Grimm and Cohen, across five samples totalling 464,229, report improved fit from a bifactor model separating judgement items from relevance items, and recommend that model rather than dropping items. Kivikangas and colleagues report that the association varies by region, by country and between White and Black respondents, and that it depends on whether the political scale is labelled social or economic. Their samples came overwhelmingly from the United States and Europe. Graham, Haidt and Nosek's own limitations section says Studies 1 to 3 were self-selected internet samples and not representative, so slopes and means should not be read as population estimates.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating the questionnaire's factor structure and the political difference as one claim. They are tested by different studies, and Harper and Rhodes' three-factor revision still separated Conservative from Labour voters. A disputed measurement model is a different situation from a failed effect. The second error is reading the headline as a within-person ranking. What Many Labs 2 tested is the correlation between self-placed ideology and the relevance of binding concerns, not whether any conservative weights five things equally. The third is assuming the whole pattern came out clean in the original. Study 3's own model gave harm and fairness betas running opposite to prediction, and Study 4's raw word counts put loyalty on the wrong side. The fourth is treating this as the same claim as partisan bias, which is measured by a different design and has its own entry. The fifth is counting the foundations as fixed at five. Iyer, Koleva, Graham, Ditto and Haidt wrote liberty items after libertarians objected that their core value was missing, and a principal component analysis of 3,732 responses split those items into economic liberty and lifestyle liberty rather than one factor. Atari, Haidt, Graham, Koleva, Stevens and Dehghani then revisited the theory using 25 populations, and their questionnaire treats equality and proportionality as distinct foundations alongside care, loyalty, authority and purity. That is six foundations, and liberty is not among them. The sixth is generalising the size of the difference from convenience data. Kivikangas and colleagues found the yourmorals.org estimates larger than those from representative samples on every foundation.
